US 10-year yield falls below 5% as investors flock to safe havens
article:
(Oct 23): US Treasuries surged — sending the US 10-year yield back below 5% — as investors sought shelter from tumbling share prices for companies leading the boom in spending on artificial intelligence (AI).

The rally trimmed yields across maturities by as much as 13 basis points (bps), with five- to 30-year yields reaching their lowest levels in nearly a month. In addition to haven demand, Treasuries benefitted from fading expectations for Federal Reserve interest-rates hikes next year.

With doubts about the sustainability of US economic growth if AI investment falters, investors flocked to bonds despite resurgent oil prices. Global benchmark Brent crude oil futures topped US$112 a barrel for the first time since May after deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns that escalating Middle East hostilities could hit supply.

“It’s really encouraging for rates that Treasuries are behaving like a safe haven asset despite the higher oil price on the day,” said Michael Chang, interest-rate derivatives strategist at Citigroup Inc.

Stock-market declines have revived the haven status of US government debt in recent weeks. Previously, the oil-driven inflation resurgence since the US started a war with Iran in late February had driven yields to multi-year highs in anticipation of additional Fed rate hikes to contain it.

See also: Indonesia eyes panda bond in November as it confronts MSCI risk — Bloomberg

Shares of US semiconductor companies — a proxy for sentiment around AI investments — resumed falling on Thursday, sending the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down as much as 6.3% to its lowest level since late July.

The path forward for the world’s largest government bond market may depend in part on whether elevated oil prices or worries about the AI stock trade gain the upper hand.

“Sentiment seems to be shakier these days as investors reconsider AI-related assets,” said Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS Bank Ltd. “With US yields still elevated by recent standards, investors may want to hedge off some of these risks by seeking safety in Treasuries.”

See also: Long-term Treasuries hold gains as oil snaps three-day rally

“Today’s price action highlights haven demand will overwhelm any worries about inflation and the Fed, if risk assets sour further. Given the higher coupon buffer to cushion total returns and still uncertain backdrop for the AI trade, bonds now hold more appeal,” says Tatiana Darie, macro strategist, Markets Live at Bloomberg Strategists.

Treasuries also benefitted along with German government bonds from the ongoing selloff in French debt. French yields across maturities reached multiyear highs, with the 10-year topping 5.14% for the first time since 2002, and they exceeded German counterparts by historically wide margins.

Despite retreating from session highs, the France’s 10-year yield exceeded Germany’s by more than 170bps, the most since 2011, when the euro debt crisis was at a fever pitch and speculation was mounting that the European Union could break apart. French financial assets have been hit by mounting investor anxiety about its debt burden and the eruption of cost-of-living protests.

The US bond rally trimmed the expected yield for an auction of five-year Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, at 1pm New York time. The auction was still poised to draw the highest yield for a five-year TIPS auction since October 2023.

A Bloomberg gauge of returns on Treasuries has climbed about 1.2% in October after rounding off its biggest monthly drop in almost two years in September.

“Even though oil has been slowly rallying, Treasuries have been feeling some safe-haven flows again,” said Kenneth Crompton, head of rates strategy at National Australia Bank.

title: US stocks drop as risk-off views dominate with oil up, Meta falling
article:
(Oct 22): US stocks declined Thursday as escalating concern about Mideast conflict pushed oil prices higher, spurring inflation fears with US midterm elections less than two weeks away. Meta Platforms Inc tumbled as investors parsed its results along with the rest of the latest batch of technology earnings for evidence that massive spending on artificial intelligence (AI) is paying off.

Tech shares led the broader stock market lower, with the Nasdaq 100 Index sliding 2.4% as of 11.19am in New York. The S&P 500 Index fell 1.3%, while West Texas Intermediate crude rose 1.1% to US$98.18 a barrel. Yields on 10-year Treasuries retreated to 5%. The US ordered some diplomats and their families out of Saudi Arabia because of the threat from Houthi militants, and at least four people were killed by attacks on an Aramco oil site and a Saudi Arabian airport on Wednesday.

“Investors should stay invested for further equity gains via broadly diversified exposure across sectors and regions,” while building resilience via fixed income and commodities, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, UBS global equities head said in a note.

Meta slid 5.9% even after reporting better-than-expected results and boosting its capital spending outlook. Shares had initially traded higher following the results, as CEO Mark Zuckerberg touted its AI agent Muse. On Thursday, a gauge of the company’s credit risk surged to a fresh record as spending plans reignited fears tech giants will issue more debt in an already-saturated market. Tesla Inc shares shed 0.78% after the electric-car maker cut its spending plans. Elevated operating expenses underscored the cost of its AI, robotics and autonomy push.

The sector faces broad threats, according to Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok. “If the AI payoff is slow to materialise or never arrives, venture capital returns would come under pressure, since the capital funding today’s token spending would have little to show for it, and a pullback in venture funding could in turn weaken demand for compute,” he warned in a note.

See also: Berkshire stock hits new high, moving on from Buffett’s exit

Chipmakers and other tech stocks fell after reports from Tesla, Lam Research Corp and IBM underwhelmed, weighing on growth sectors and pushing cryptocurrency-linked names lower. Lam Research’s weaker-than-expected guidance weighed on the broader chip-equipment complex, overshadowing a beat from Texas Instruments Inc. Apple Inc rose 0.2%.

If losses in technology stocks hold until the close, the Nasdaq 100 will post its worst day since June. The tech-heavy index is eyeing a fourth day of a move of at least 1% in either direction in five sessions.

See also: Nasdaq 100 climbs as SpaceX results fuel AI trade

Developments in Europe also spurred unease, as French bond stress deepened with investors ditching riskier assets around the world. “German bunds and US Treasuries are the flight to safety trade in the face of this, for now,” Peter Boockvar, author of The Boock Report, wrote in a note. He expects that “at least in the short term, yields in the US have seen a temporary peak.”
• Financials and real estate, as Blackstone Inc reported assets under management and real-estate assets under management that fell short of estimates.
• Airlines, after American Airlines Group Inc forecast a wider-than-anticipated quarterly loss per share and said it expects higher fuel expenses. On Wednesday, United Airlines Holdings Inc forecast weaker-than-expected earnings, underscoring how soaring jet fuel prices are eating into airline profits despite resilient demand for travel.
• Homebuilders, after PulteGroup Inc missed estimates, with chief executive officer Ryan Marshall saying that “the rapid increase in interest rates has stretched affordability even further, made selling an existing home even harder, and has pushed even more consumers to the sidelines.”
• Retreating yields on 10-year Treasuries, which are linked with mortgage rates, may offer some support for real estate companies.
• Consumer staples, after better-than-expected results from bellwether Procter & Gamble Co, along with appetite for defensive names after lackluster tech reports.
• Memory stocks, with broader weakness in AI-linked companies. Western Digital Corp is expected to report earnings after the close.
• Crypto stocks, as Bitcoin drops below US$82,000 on AI jitters.

Treasury unveils rules banning large investors from buying homes
article:
(Oct 22): The US Treasury Department on Thursday proposed new regulations to bar large institutional investors from buying up single-family homes, the latest step in the process to implement the most controversial section of the sweeping bipartisan housing law passed this summer.

 

Under the law, the ban — which prohibits investors with more than 350 houses from purchasing additional single-family homes — goes into effect on Jan 7, a short runway Treasury acknowledged in the 96-page proposal.

“Given this short implementation period and the need for market participants to make decisions regarding homebuilding, acquisitions, ownership structures, investment arrangements, and compliance systems, Treasury currently intends to take a phased rulemaking approach,” the agency said.

The institutional investor restrictions were part of a populist affordability pitch by President Donald Trump, who declared, “People live in homes, not corporations.”

Critics have argued, though, that the policy could create a chilling effect for builders, and in turn, be a drag on supply.

Market participants were still reviewing the proposal on Thursday morning.

“This is a very complicated provision and a very complicated rule as a result of that,” said David Dworkin, president and chief executive officer of the National Housing Conference. “The bottom line is going to be whether the market continues to build desperately needed rental housing or not. And if we see that builders continue to construct rental housing, regardless of whether it is stacked on top of each other or side by side, I think that Treasury successfully navigated the issue.”

See also: US housing starts fall to four-month low as demand falters

“If on the other hand the market stops investing in rental housing, then what we’ve done is simply exacerbated the affordable housing crisis,” Dworkin added.

The bipartisan housing law aimed to alleviate a supply crunch that has contributed to voters’ frustrations over affordability. In addition to the institutional investor restriction, the law includes new rules making it easier to develop factory-built housing and encouraging localities to remove barriers to construction.

title: Taiwan’s US$5 tril stock market to close on Friday as Typhoon Champi nears
article:
(Oct 22): Taiwan’s stock exchange will shut on Friday as Typhoon Champi approaches the island, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds and prompting authorities to shut offices and schools in capital city Taipei.

While the storm has weakened from super typhoon strength, its top sustained winds remain at 213km (132 miles) per hour, equivalent to a Category 4 hurricane. The storm reached super typhoon strength earlier this week, making it the 10th to reach that level in the northwest Pacific Ocean this season.

That’s double the long-term average and just shy of a record 13 in 2015 — also an El Nino year, according to the Hong Kong Observatory. Storms tend to form farther east during the climate phenomenon, giving a cyclone more time to accumulate energy over open and warm waters as it churns towards land.

“The 185 miles per hour peak is behind us,” said James Caron, director of meteorological operations for North America and Asia at Atmospheric G2, referring to Champi’s earlier intensity that made it one of the world’s post powerful storms this year. “The risks that matter now are rain and the size of the wind field, not peak wind.”

Taiwan’s stock exchange is the fifth-largest globally, with a market capitalisation of more than US$5 trillion. It is also closed Monday for a holiday, leaving the island with an added trading gap versus others in the region.

The tech-heavy stock market, along with South Korea and Japan, has seen selloffs in recent sessions as investors track earnings from global tech giants. The Taiwan dollar also weakened this week, weighed down by foreign capital outflows.

See also: Chinese stocks enter bear market as tech slumps, policy hopes ebb

title: US agrees to buy at least 850 more F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed
article:
(Oct 22): The Pentagon plans to buy at least 850 additional Lockheed Martin Corp F-35 fighter jets, in what would be the biggest contract in the programme’s quarter-century history that signals the stealth warplane will remain a major part of the US arsenal for many years.

The contract, which is not yet final, also includes procurement of initial spare parts and modification kits, plus sustainment of the global F-35 fleet over 10 years, the Defense Department said in a statement on Thursday morning.

The Pentagon statement did not provide a value for the contract. The jet, which has three variants, costs about US$100 million each. Lockheed Martin will self-fund “at least US$7 billion in initiatives that support” the programme, the Pentagon added.

The framework is intended to stabilise prices, insure adequate spare parts supplies and improved reliability in the face of emerging threats like artificial intelligence and drones.

Many US fourth-generation jets, like F-15s and F-16s, have been in service for decades and will be retired before the next generation F-47 and F/A-XX aircraft are in production.

The renewed award is a vote of confidence in the F-35, after the aircraft became a prime target of criticism under President Donald Trump. Elon Musk said in late 2024 that “some idiots are still building manned fighter jets like the F-35” in a new era of warfare focused on autonomous flight.

See also: American Airlines cuts outlook again, sees higher fuel bill this year

Previous F-35 contracts have been finalised in “blocks” typically of three years, but Lockheed Martin, which 25 years ago this month won a contest with Boeing Co to build the fighter, has for years sought a larger, multi-year contract because it almost guarantees — subject to annual congressional appropriations — a stable revenue stream and orders for hundreds of subcontractors.

In this case, the framework calls for producing 156 jets per year over a decade. The US this year approved similar deals to increase production of critical munitions such as air defence interceptors.

“We have fundamentally changed how we stabilise the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” Under Secretary for Acquisition Michael Duffey said in a statement on Thursday. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it.”

See also: Boeing wins US approval for largest variant of 737 Max jet

Lockheed Martin president and chief executive officer Jim Taiclet said in a statement that “with the greater certainty that comes from the US government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.”

“In the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work to finalise contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal contract award,” the company said.

The US midterm elections in just a few weeks might give Democrats control of Congress, however, which may change spending plans as new lawmakers take up budgets.

The F-35 programme has been hampered by repeated instances of low combat readiness or “mission capable rates” and major delays delivering a new software and hardware upgrade called TR3.

The cost of the warplane programme — already the most expensive in US history — has risen by about US$51 billion, or roughly 10%, since late 2023 because of software, readiness, spare parts and engine power improvements.

More than 1,375 F-35s are in service with militaries around the world — most with the US — and the fleet has surpassed a million flight hours. The warplane has also flown numerous missions during the war with Iran.

The F-35 “is the foundation of the Air Force’s fighter force structure,” the service said in a report to Congress last Friday on the service’s long-range fighter plans.

Lockheed Martin “continues to produce and modernize F-35s for the Air Force but is currently delivering aircraft with significant combat system gaps,” according to the report, obtained by Bloomberg News.

Boeing was chosen to build both the F-47 and F/A-XX, while Northrop Grumman Corp is producing the next-generation US bomber, the B-21 Raider.

title: American Airlines cuts outlook again, sees higher fuel bill this year
article:
(Oct 22): American Airlines Group Inc cut its full-year outlook again and issued a wide range for its fourth-quarter loss target, highlighting how the industry is struggling to predict its performance amid persistently high fuel prices.

 

The range for the final three months stretches from an adjusted loss of 50 cents a share to as much as US$1.10, American said in a statement on Thursday. That compares with analyst estimates of a 49-cent deficit for the quarter. The shares fell 2.9% in pre-market trading.

The airline said it incurred a US$1.9 billion increase in fuel expense, and the cost will be about US$2.8 billion higher in the fourth quarter than a year earlier. The carrier has warned that it may need to further reduce flying if prices remain elevated, echoing rivals that are prioritising profitability over market share.

American Airlines reduced its full-year earnings goal for a third time in the past six months. The company now predicts an adjusted loss per share of US$1 to US$1.60, compared with a guidance in July that ranged from a 65-cent loss to a 65-cent profit.

American joins other major US airlines including United Airlines Holdings Inc and Delta Air Lines Inc in reporting disappointing earnings as higher fuel costs erodes profits, though strong demand, particularly among wealthier travellers, has provided a measure of relief to the industry.

Premium revenue increased by about 23%, and main cabin revenue increased 20% year over year. That strength mirrors trends at its major rivals who have led the industry in capturing premium travellers across the country. United saw premium revenue climb 17% in the third quarter, while Delta saw an increase of 18% year over year.

American has been navigating a spate of operational and strategic challenges, from slashing its debt load to trying to win back corporate flyers alienated by an unpopular marketing strategy. The carrier said ended the third quarter with US$11.8 billion of total available cash and more than US$26 billion in debt.

See also: Boeing wins US approval for largest variant of 737 Max jet

Adding to the carrier’s efforts to compete with its rivals is American’s plan to extend Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service to more than 1,000 mainline aircraft, as US carriers compete to offer faster in-flight WiFi.

The airline plans to equip its entire mainline fleet, including Airbus and Boeing narrowbody jets and widebody aircraft, with the high-speed service beginning in early 2027. The expanded agreement more than doubles American’s initial commitment announced in May to install Starlink on more than 500 Airbus aircraft.

The move comes as Starlink, owned by Musk’s SpaceX, has emerged as a key battleground among the largest US airlines, which are increasingly touting faster connectivity to lure passengers from rivals. American joins United and Southwest Airlines Co in embracing the technology.

title: Bosch to separate auto-parts unit as Chinese rivals gain ground
article:
(Oct 22): Robert Bosch plans to legally separate its automotive-parts business, as the world’s largest car supplier races to cut costs and respond to intensifying competition from China.

Bosch Mobility will be transferred out of the German parent company into a separate limited-liability company while remaining wholly-owned by the Bosch group, it said Thursday.

The privately held group also plans to split out its Bosch Digital, Global Business Services and Global Real Estate operations, turning the existing entity primarily into a holding company that will also house the central research and advanced engineering team.

The reorganisation marks a break for a company that grew from Robert Bosch’s 1886 Stuttgart workshop into an automotive giant built on spark plugs, fuel injection and brakes. As value shifts toward electric-vehicle batteries, software and artificial intelligence, Chinese suppliers including CATL and Huawei are gaining ground. Meanwhile, major European customers such as Volkswagen AG and Stellantis NV are cutting costs and struggling.

“We are operating in an increasingly challenging environment across our markets,” chairman Christian Fischer said in a statement. “New competitors, particularly from Asia, are intensifying the competitive pressure.”

The new structure will mean the car-parts business can “respond more quickly to market trends in the future and align its operations even more consistently with new customer needs,” he said.

See also: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs in AI-fuelled push to lower costs

Bosch currently has no plans to list or sell Mobility, or combine it with another auto supplier, a spokesman said.

The restructuring goes a step beyond an overhaul that began in 2024, when Bosch gave its sprawling Mobility business its own leadership team and greater responsibility for its operations. Bosch said at the time that the shift toward software-defined vehicles required it to serve customers faster and organise around areas including software, semiconductors and vehicle computers.

The pressure is particularly acute in auto parts. Mobility generated €55.8 billion (US$65 billion or $83 billion) of sales last year, more than 60% of Bosch’s total, but its operating margin sank to 1.8% from 3.8% a year earlier. Bosch has said it needs to close an annual cost gap of about €2.5 billion to reach its profitability target.

See also: Westpac axes 140 more roles as Australia bank job cuts intensify

The Mobility business accounts for more than half of the 413,000 people employed by the Bosch group at the end of 2025.

Chinese competition is helping reset benchmarks for both price and development speed. Huawei is investing heavily in smart-driving technology as it expands as a supplier of software, computing and cockpit systems, while CATL dominates global EV batteries. That leaves established suppliers needing to spend heavily on new technology, even as automakers squeeze them harder on price.

Bosch is already cutting deeply to close the gap. The company announced plans last year to eliminate about 13,000 jobs, largely in Mobility, after weakening orders and lower-than-expected demand for EVs intensified pressure on the business.

The problems have persisted this year. Mobility sales slipped slightly to €27.8 billion in the first half, and Bosch has warned that tough auto markets are likely to persist as it tries to make its largest business more competitive.
